questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: A Running Product From One Pass
questions.learningObjective: trace an accumulating product and read two figures derived from it
questions.stem:
A five-element list of positive integers is reduced in one pass to a running product, and two figures are then read off that product list. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. Which line of output does it produce?

import itertools
import operator

vals = [1, 2, 3, 4, 5]
out = list(itertools.accumulate(vals, operator.mul))
print(out)
print(len(out))
print(out[-1] // out[0])
print(out[3] - out[2])

options.text: A list of five running products, then one hundred and twenty from the last value divided by the first, then eighteen from the fourth less the third
A list of four running products that start at two, sixty from the last divided by the first, then ninety six from the fourth less the third
options.misconception: believes the accumulator starts empty so the first value never reaches the output

options.text: A list of four neighbouring products, ten from the last divided by the first, then eight from the fourth less the third
options.misconception: believes the two-argument operation joins neighbours rather than the running total

options.text: The original list of five values, a length of five, then five from the last divided by the first, then one from the fourth less the third
options.misconception: believes the running products are built but never returned

questions.explanation: The step receives two arguments every time: the total carried so far and the next value, and each call returns the new total that replaces the old one. The first call therefore pairs nothing with the first value, so the first entry of the output is the first input and the output is as long as the input. From one the running products are one, two, six, twenty four, one hundred and twenty. The last over the first is one hundred and twenty over one, and the gap between the fourth and the third is twenty four less six. The answer that starts at two is the belief that a running total has no seed: a step with two arguments cannot produce anything from one value alone.
questions.hint: Ask what the first call of a two-argument step receives as its left argument.

questions.topic: What A Default Accumulator Leaves Out
questions.learningObjective: say what a reduction emits when no step function is supplied
questions.stem:
A list of five readings is reduced with the accumulator called without a step function. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does that call produce, and what does it leave out?

import itertools

readings = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5]
totals = list(itertools.accumulate(readings))
print(totals)
print(len(totals), len(readings))

options.text: One total, the sum of the whole list, because a reduction collapses everything in a single pass and emits only the final value
options.misconception: believes a reduction emits only its last value

options.text: Five running totals whose first entry is the first reading on its own, because the default step simply adds and the first call has nothing to add to
Six running totals whose first entry is a zero, because a default starting value of zero is emitted in front of the totals the step then produces
options.misconception: believes a zero seed is emitted as the first running total

options.text: Four running totals, because the default step needs a pair of values before it can produce anything at all
options.misconception: believes a running total cannot be produced from a single input

questions.explanation: With no step function the call supplies addition as the step, so the emitted sequence is the prefix sums of the input. The first emission is the first reading itself, because the step is only invoked from the second element onward, and there is no zero in front of it unless one is asked for. That is why the output is exactly as long as the input, five and five here. The variant that inserts a leading zero asks for a different call, one given a starting value, and it pays for the seed by making the output one element longer than the input.
questions.hint: Count how many times the step runs when the list has five elements and no seed is given.

questions.topic: Groups Split Only On A Value Change
questions.learningObjective: group a run of equal values and total each run in one pass
questions.stem:
A word is split into runs of equal letters, and each run is counted and the counts totalled. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

import itertools

word = "aabbc"
report = []
for letter, run in itertools.groupby(word):
    report.append((letter, len(list(run))))
print(report)
print(len(report))
print(sum(n for _, n in report))

options.text: Five groups of one letter each, a group count of five, and a total of five, because a new group is started at every position rather than only on a change of value
options.misconception: believes grouping starts a new group at every value

options.text: Two groups of two b and one c, a group count of two, and a total of three, because a new group is started only when a letter repeats itself
options.misconception: believes a new group is started on a repeat rather than on a change

options.text: Three groups of two a, two b and one c, a group count of three, and a total of five, because a group is a run of equal values and the run lengths add back to the word length
Three groups of two a, two b and one c, a group count of three, and a total of three, because the final line adds one per group rather than the run lengths
options.misconception: believes the total counts groups instead of the letters inside them

questions.explanation: The grouping walks the input once and starts a new group exactly when the current value differs from the previous one, so the number of groups equals the number of runs and the run lengths always add back up to the length of the input. In this word the runs are two a, two b and one c, there are three of them, and two plus two plus one is five. The answer that totals three is the arithmetic slip to watch for: the run has to be drained before its length is known, and a length taken after draining is the length of that run, not a running position. The answer that starts a group at every value is the belief that grouping is a partition rather than a run detector.
questions.hint: Add up the lengths of the runs and compare that with the length of the word.

questions.topic: A Grouping Key That Answers The Wrong Question
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a grouping key that tests membership instead of equality
questions.stem:
A program is supposed to count each run of equal letters, but the report it builds does not describe the word. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What is the fault, and what does it actually print?

import itertools

word = "aabbc"
report = []
for flag, run in itertools.groupby(word, key=lambda ch: ch in "aeiou"):
    report.append((flag, len(list(run))))
print(report)
print(sum(n for _, n in report))

options.text: The key is evaluated once per group rather than once per value, so the runs split apart, and the report is five entries of one letter each for a total of five
options.misconception: believes the grouping key is evaluated per group and not per element

options.text: The key is missing altogether, so nothing is grouped at all, the report is empty and the total is zero because no comparison was ever made
options.misconception: believes omitting the key compares whole words instead of values

options.text: The key upper-cases each letter by accident, so the report is the same two runs under upper-case names, two and two and one for a total of five
options.misconception: believes case folding is applied to the grouping key

options.text: The key returns a truth value rather than the letter, so the two a form a single group and the two b together with the c form the other, and the report is true two then false three for a total of five

questions.explanation: The grouping compares the values the key returns, not the original values, so a key that answers a yes-or-no question turns the grouping into one that runs by truth value. Two vowels and then three consonants are two runs, and the total is still five, which is the trap here: a total that comes out right does not prove the grouping was right. The report shows a boolean where a letter should be, so the output cannot be read back to the word. To group by letter the key has to return the letter, and then the same total comes back with the same two plus two plus one, this time attached to the letters it describes.
questions.hint: Ask what the key returns, and what the grouping then compares when it looks for a change.

questions.topic: Overlapping Windows From One List
questions.learningObjective: build the overlapping adjacent pairs of a sequence
questions.stem:
Three readings are turned into every overlapping pair of adjacent readings, and the gaps inside those pairs are listed. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

import itertools

vals = [10, 20, 30]
pairs = list(itertools.pairwise(vals))
print(pairs)
print(len(pairs))
print([b - a for a, b in pairs])

options.text: Two overlapping pairs ten twenty and twenty thirty, a count of two, and gaps of ten and ten, because the window advances a single place at a time
One pair of ten and twenty, a count of one, and a single gap of ten, because the window advances by the width of the window and the tail is left over
options.misconception: believes the window advances by its own width

options.text: Three pairs including a wrap-around thirty and ten, a count of three, and gaps of ten, ten and negative twenty, because the sequence is treated as circular
options.misconception: believes the last window wraps around to the first

options.text: Two overlapping pairs ten twenty and twenty thirty, a count of two, and gaps of ten and twenty, because each window is measured from the first value rather than from its neighbour
options.misconception: believes the gap inside a window is measured from the first value

questions.explanation: The call takes a window of width two and slides it along by one position at a time, so three values give two overlapping windows and the middle value appears in both. Nothing is discarded between windows, and the sequence is not treated as circular, so the last window stops at the final value. The number of windows for a sequence of length n is n minus one, which is the figure to check the output against: two windows here. The gaps are measured inside each window, so both come out as ten, and an answer that measures from the first value has silently changed what the pair means.
questions.hint: For a sequence of length n, how many width-two windows fit if the window moves one place at a time?

questions.topic: A Fill Value Where One List Runs Out
questions.learningObjective: pair sequences of unequal length using an explicit fill
questions.stem:
Two sequences of different lengths are zipped together, and a fill value stands in for the missing entries. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

import itertools

names = ["ada", "bob", "cy"]
tags = ["x", "y"]
rows = list(itertools.zip_longest(names, tags, fillvalue="-"))
print(rows)
print(len(rows))
print(rows[-1][1])

options.text: Three rows where the last row is cy against an absent marker, a row count of three, and an absent marker as the second field of the last row, because the fill was left at its own default
options.misconception: believes the shortest form is used with an empty marker

options.text: Three rows where the last row is cy against a fill, a row count of three, and a fill as the second field of the last row, because the longer sequence decides how many rows there are
Two rows, a row count of two, and y as the second field of the last row, because a zip stops as soon as the shorter sequence is used up
options.misconception: believes a zip always stops at the shorter sequence

options.text: Three rows where every row is a fill against a fill, a row count of three, and a fill as the second field of the last row, because the fill replaces the entry that does exist as well
options.misconception: believes the fill substitutes for the surviving entry too

questions.explanation: The longest-call form of a zip runs until the longest input is used up, and the fill value is substituted only where an input has nothing left to give. Here the names run one past the tags, so exactly one field is filled and the third name survives. The number of rows is the length of the longest input, three. The plain form of a zip does the opposite: it stops at the shortest input and silently discards the surplus, which is the mistake the fill exists to prevent. Omitting the fill altogether does not stop the zip either, it just reports the missing entries as an empty marker instead of a chosen value.
questions.hint: Ask which input decides the number of rows when the two have different lengths.

questions.topic: A Zip That Was Told To Check
questions.learningObjective: read the failure raised when a strict zip is given unequal inputs
questions.stem:
Two sequences of unequal length are zipped with the strict option switched on, so a length mismatch is meant to be reported rather than hidden. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. It does not finish normally. What reaches the screen, and what stops it?

rows = list(zip([1, 2], [3, 4, 5], strict=True))
print(rows)

options.text: Nothing at all, and the interpreter stops with a type error saying the zip got an unexpected keyword argument, because the option name is not accepted
options.misconception: believes the option name is rejected rather than obeyed

options.text: Nothing at all, and the interpreter stops with a value error saying the lengths differ and naming two against three, because the message comes from the program rather than from the zip
options.misconception: believes the message is written by the program rather than by the zip

options.text: Nothing at all, and the interpreter stops with a value error saying the second argument is longer than the first
The two pairs one three and two four, and the run finishes normally, because an option that was not understood is ignored and the zip truncates as usual
options.misconception: believes an unrecognised option is ignored

questions.explanation: The strict option changes the zip from a truncating one into a checking one, and the check happens as the inputs are pulled, before the list reaches the print. So the print line never appears and the only text the run produces is the error naming which argument ran out first. The message is asymmetric on purpose: it names the argument that is longer rather than stating a comparison, because the shorter one is the one that ended. Passing a false value switches the check back off, and passing a misspelled name or a value of the wrong type fails earlier, for a different reason.
questions.hint: Decide whether the pairs are collected into a list before the lengths are compared.

questions.topic: Batches Of A Fixed Size With A Short Tail
questions.learningObjective: split a sequence into fixed-size batches and read the short last batch
questions.stem:
Five readings are cut into batches of two, keeping the short final batch instead of dropping it, and the batch sizes are reported. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3, where the batching call arrived in version 3.12. What does it print?

import itertools

vals = [10, 20, 30, 40, 50]
batches = [list(b) for b in itertools.batched(vals, 2)]
print(batches)
print([len(b) for b in batches])
print(sum(len(b) for b in batches))

options.text: Two batches of two each, sizes two and two, and a total of four, because a partial final batch is dropped from the result
options.misconception: believes a short final batch is discarded

options.text: Two batches of two each, sizes two and two, and a total of four, because the input is truncated to a multiple of the batch width first
options.misconception: believes the input is trimmed to a whole number of batches

options.text: A single batch holding all five values, a size of five, and a total of five, because the width argument is treated as a hint rather than as a block size
options.misconception: believes the width argument is advisory

options.text: Batches of ten and twenty, then thirty and forty, then a last batch holding only fifty, sizes two two and one, and a total of five, because the remainder is kept as a shorter final batch

questions.explanation: Batching cuts the input into consecutive runs of the given width and hands back the last run even when it is short, so five values at width two give two full batches and a tail of one. The sum of the batch lengths is therefore the length of the input, five, which is the cheapest way to check the split. The drop-the-tail behaviour is what a slice-and-step loop did, and it loses data silently at the end of every stream, which is the belief behind the answers of four. The width argument is not a hint: it is what makes the output blocks, and every batch but the last is exactly that wide.
questions.hint: Divide the length of the input by the batch width and look at the remainder.

questions.topic: An Unbounded Count Cut To Four
questions.learningObjective: stop an endless counter after a fixed number of values
questions.stem:
An endless counter that climbs by three each step is cut to its first four values, and the last of them is checked against a closed form. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

import itertools

vals = list(itertools.islice(itertools.count(1, 3), 4))
print(vals)
print(vals[-1])
print(vals[-1] == 1 + 3 * (len(vals) - 1))

options.text: The values one, four, seven and ten, a last value of ten, and a true check, because the stop is a count of values and four of them were taken
The values one, four, seven, ten and thirteen, a last value of thirteen, and a true check, because the stop count includes the value sitting at that position
options.misconception: believes the stop count includes the value at that index

options.text: The values zero, three, six and nine, a last value of nine, and a true check, because the counter is measured in positions rather than in values
options.misconception: believes the slice reports positions counted from zero

options.text: The values one, four, seven and ten, a last value of ten, and a false check, because the closed form subtracts one from the count twice over
options.misconception: believes the closed form check double-counts the off-by-one

questions.explanation: The counter is endless, so the only thing that decides when the list is finished is the slice, and the slice stop is a count of values rather than a value to reach. Four values are taken, which are one, four, seven and ten, and the last is the start plus the step times one fewer than the number of values. That is why ten rather than thirteen: thirteen would be the fifth value, and the stop count of four has already been reached. The general rule worth keeping is that any endless source can be cut this way, and the last value is always start plus step times count minus one.
questions.hint: Write the last value as the start plus the step times one fewer than the number of values taken.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: Tallies And The Ties They Break
questions.learningObjective: rank tallies and explain how equal counts are ordered
questions.stem:
A word is tallied by letter, the two most common letters are listed, a key that was never counted is asked for, and the counts are totalled. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

from collections import Counter

tally = Counter("aassii")
print(tally)
print(tally.most_common(2))
print(tally["s"], tally["z"])
print(sum(tally.values()))

options.text: The tally of a two, s two and i two, the top two as a then s, a hit of two and a miss of zero, and a grand total of three counting the distinct letters
options.misconception: believes the total counts distinct letters rather than occurrences

options.text: The tally of a two, s two and i two, the top two as a then s, a hit of two and a miss of zero, and a grand total of six
The tally of a two, s two and i two, the top two as a then i, a hit of two and a miss of zero, and a grand total of six
options.misconception: believes a tie between equal counts is broken alphabetically

options.text: The tally of a two, s two and i two, the top two as a then s, a hit of two and a miss reported as an absent marker, and a grand total of six
options.misconception: believes a tally miss reports an absent marker rather than a zero

questions.explanation: A tally table counts occurrences, and asking for a key that was never counted gives zero rather than raising, so the miss on z is a plain zero. The three letters each appear twice, which is six in total, and every key ties. The ranking sorts by count alone, so the tie is settled by the order the letters were first counted, which is the order they appear in the word: a, then s, then i. Alphabetical order happens to agree for a and s only because a does come first in the word, and the answer that reports a then i is the one that shows the difference, since i is the letter that sorts after s and was counted last.
questions.hint: Check the letter positions in the word, and check whether the ranking looks at anything but the count.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: What A Tally Table Does With A Miss
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a tally lookup from an ordinary mapping lookup
questions.stem:
A tally table is built from a list of tags and then queried for a tag that never appeared. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does the query report, and what follows from that?

from collections import Counter

tally = Counter(["red", "blue", "red"])
print(tally["red"])
print(tally["green"])
print("green" in tally)
print(tally.most_common(1))

options.text: A count of two for the tag that appeared, a count of zero for a tag that never appeared, a membership test that is now true, and the top pair as red twice
options.misconception: believes reading a tally inserts the key into the table

options.text: A count of two for the tag that appeared, a count of one for a tag that never appeared, a membership test that is now true, and the top pair as red twice
options.misconception: believes a missing tally starts at one and is then recorded

options.text: A count of two for the tag that appeared, a count of zero for a tag that never appeared, a membership test that is false, and the top pair as red twice
A count of two for the tag that appeared and then a raised lookup error for a tag that never appeared, because a tally is an ordinary mapping underneath
options.misconception: believes a tally raises on a missing key like an ordinary mapping

questions.explanation: A tally table is a mapping with one difference: reading a key that was never counted yields zero instead of raising. That is the whole reason to reach for a tally rather than an ordinary table, because counting code can ask about anything without first checking whether it exists. Membership is still the ordinary test, so a tag that was never counted is not in the table, which is what the false result means. Reading does not insert, and the ranking is over the keys that were actually counted, so red at two is the only pair reported.
questions.hint: Ask whether reading a tally table creates the key, and what the membership test reports for it.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: Subtraction Drops Non-Positive Counts
questions.learningObjective: predict which letters survive a difference of two tallies
questions.stem:
Two tallies of the same letters are subtracted, and the letters that survive are reported. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

from collections import Counter

a = Counter("abbbc")
b = Counter("abc")
diff = a - b
print(sorted(diff.items()))
print("a" in diff, "b" in diff, "c" in diff)
print(len(diff))
print(sum(diff.values()))

options.text: Pairs of a zero, b two and c zero, membership true for all three, a length of three, and a leftover total of two, because a key that reaches zero is still kept
options.misconception: believes a key whose count reaches zero is kept

options.text: Pairs of a zero, b of a negative count and c zero, membership true for all three, a length of three, and a leftover total that comes out negative, because the counts are subtracted with no floor applied
options.misconception: believes the difference is allowed to go negative

options.text: Pairs of a one, b one and c one, membership true for all three, a length of three, and a leftover total of three, because a shared key is reduced to the smaller of both tallies
options.misconception: believes a difference keeps the smaller count instead

options.text: A single pair of b two, membership false for a, true for b and false for c, a length of one, and a leftover total of two, because counts that do not stay positive are dropped

questions.explanation: Subtracting two tallies keeps only the counts that come out strictly positive, so letters that were consumed entirely or that were not present to begin with disappear from the result. Here a appears once against once, c once against once, and b three against one, so only b survives with a count of two, the difference has one key, and the counts that are left add to two. A key that reached zero is not the same as a key that was never present, and neither is kept. That rule is what makes the difference usable for set-style questions such as which items remain unmatched, and it is why a hand-rolled subtraction loop that leaves zeros behind gives a different answer for the same data.
questions.hint: Subtract the counts yourself and then ask which results are strictly greater than zero.

questions.topic: A Duration Taken Apart Into Its Parts
questions.learningObjective: read a normalised duration and its part fields
questions.stem:
A duration is built from days, hours and seconds in one call, and its normalised parts are printed. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

import datetime

span = datetime.timedelta(days=2, hours=3, seconds=-1)
print(span)
print(span.days)
print(span.seconds)
print(span.total_seconds())
print(span // datetime.timedelta(hours=12))

options.text: A duration shown as two days and two hours fifty nine minutes and fifty nine seconds, a day part of two, a seconds part of ten thousand seven hundred and ninety nine, a total of one hundred and eighty three thousand five hundred and ninety nine seconds, and a quotient of four whole half-day units

A duration shown as two days and two hours fifty nine minutes and fifty nine seconds, a day part of two, a seconds part of three thousand five hundred and ninety nine, a total of one hundred and eighty three thousand five hundred and ninety nine seconds, and a quotient of four whole half-day units
options.misconception: believes the seconds part holds the leftover seconds within the hour

options.text: A duration shown as two days and fifty hours fifty nine minutes and fifty nine seconds, a day part of two, a seconds part of ten thousand seven hundred and ninety nine, a total of one hundred and eighty three thousand five hundred and ninety nine seconds, and a quotient of four whole half-day units
options.misconception: believes the hours can run past the end of a day

options.text: A duration shown as two days and two hours fifty nine minutes and fifty nine seconds, a day part of two, a seconds part of fifty nine, a total of one hundred and eighty three thousand five hundred and ninety nine seconds, and a quotient of four whole half-day units
options.misconception: believes the seconds part holds only the seconds of the minute

questions.explanation: A duration is normalised the moment it is built, and normalisation is why a negative second does not survive as a negative field. Two days plus three hours less one second is two days, two hours, fifty nine minutes and fifty nine seconds, which is one second short of two days three hours. The day part therefore reads two, and the seconds part is the leftover seconds within the day, ten thousand seven hundred and ninety nine, not the leftover seconds within the hour or within the minute. Dividing the duration by a half-day unit gives four whole units, because dividing one duration by another truncates towards zero.
questions.hint: Rewrite the duration as two days and three hours, take away one second, and renormalise.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: A Factory That Joins Where It Should Count
questions.learningObjective: diagnose a default factory of the wrong shape for the job
questions.stem:
A program counts how many times each of several words occurs, using a table whose default factory builds an empty list. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What goes wrong, and what does it actually print?

from collections import defaultdict

words = ["ab", "b", "ab", "c"]
counts = defaultdict(list)
for w in words:
    counts[w].append(w)
print(len(counts))
print(counts["ab"])
print(len(counts["ab"]))

options.text: The table holds three keys, the value for ab holds two copies of ab, and what gets reported is the joined text abab, because a collected list is joined before it is reported
options.misconception: believes a list value is joined into text before it is reported

options.text: The factory builds a list rather than a number, so the table holds three keys, the value for ab is a list holding two copies of ab, and its length is two
The factory is never reached because the loop body does nothing useful, so the table is empty, the value for ab is an empty list, and its length is zero
options.misconception: believes a key has to be inserted before the factory can be used

options.text: The table holds three keys, but each value is the bare word rather than a list, so what gets reported is ab itself, because the loop writes the word straight into the table
options.misconception: believes the loop writes the word straight into the table

questions.explanation: A default table stores whatever its factory builds, and the factory decides the type of every value in the table. Building a list means the table is a grouping, so appending accumulates words under each word and the value for ab is a list holding two copies of ab, of length two. If the program wanted a count it needed a factory that builds a number, either a tally table or a default of zero that is then increased. The fault is not in the loop, which behaves exactly as written, but in choosing a factory whose shape does not match what the loop stores, and the table accepts the wrong type without complaint.
questions.hint: Decide what type the factory produces and what type the loop body writes into the table.

options.text: The boolean reaches the generic handler, the float reaches the integer handler because a whole number is an integer, the bytes and the list reach the generic handler, and the string reaches its own handler
options.misconception: believes a whole valued float counts as an integer

options.text: Every value reaches the last handler that was registered, because a later registration replaces the earlier ones

options.misconception: believes a boolean is not a kind of integer

questions.explanation: The dispatcher looks at the type of the value, finds the most specific handler registered for that type or one of its ancestors, and calls it. A boolean is a kind of integer in this language, so it finds the integer handler rather than the generic one, which is the single most surprising line in the output. The float is not a kind of integer even when its value is whole, so it falls through to the generic handler, and the same is true of the bytes and the list. questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: How A Dispatcher Chooses Among Types
questions.learningObjective: explain the rule a type dispatcher applies to choose a handler

answer.exemplar: The dispatcher keeps a table from a type to the function that should handle values of that type, and the entry is not filled in for every type in existence: the exact type gets the function registered for it, and anything with no entry of its own falls back to the generic function. That is why asking for the integer entry gives the integer function, asking for the string entry gives the string function, and asking for the float entry gives the generic function under its own name, because nobody registered anything for a float. The important rule is that dispatch looks along the inheritance chain, not only at the exact type. A value whose type is a subclass of a registered type finds that registration, which is why a boolean is handled as an integer, and a subclass of a registered type is handled by the same function unless something closer has been registered for it. The practical consequence is that a handler can be added after the generic function is declared, which is what makes the pattern usable for extending behaviour without editing the original function.

questions.explanation: The table has one entry per type that was registered, and reading the entry for a type that was never registered gives the generic function rather than a failure. That is the whole selection rule: exact match first, then the inheritance chain, then the generic function as the floor. The reason a boolean reaches the integer handler is the same rule applied one level up, since a boolean is a kind of integer even though nobody registered a handler for it. Because registration happens after the generic function exists, new behaviour can be added without editing it, and the table is the place to look when a value is not being handled the way it was expected to be.
questions.hint: Ask what the table holds for a type nobody registered anything for.

questions.learningObjective: sort records with a reusable field accessor
questions.stem:
Three two-field rows are sorted twice with a reusable accessor, and the accessor is also used to read two positions at once. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

import operator

rows = [("b", 2), ("a", 3), ("c", 1)]
print(sorted(rows, key=operator.itemgetter(0)))
print(sorted(rows, key=operator.itemgetter(1), reverse=True))
print(operator.itemgetter(0, 1)(("x", "y", "z")))
print(operator.itemgetter(1)([9, 8, 7]))

options.text: The first sort gives a, b, c and the second gives c, b, a, the two positions give x and y, and a single position gives eight, because a descending sort reverses the order
options.misconception: believes a descending sort reverses the ascending order of a different field

options.text: The first sort gives a, b, c and the second gives a, b, c, the two positions give y and x, and a single position gives eight, because the positions are read right to left
options.misconception: believes a multi-position accessor reads right to left

options.text: The first sort gives a, b, c and the second gives a, b, c, the two positions give x and y, and a single position gives nine, because a single accessor starts at the first position
options.misconception: believes a single accessor starts at position zero

options.text: Both sorts come out as a, b, c, the two positions give x and y, and a single position gives eight, because a descending sort by the number reverses into the same order as the ascending sort by the letter

questions.explanation: The accessor is called once per row and returns the field the sort compares, so sorting by position zero orders the rows by their letter and sorting by position one orders them by their number. Descending by the number gives three, two, one, which is the same order as ascending by the letter here, and that coincidence is the trap: the two sorts happen to agree because the data was chosen that way, not because the sort ignores the direction. An accessor built with two positions returns both values in the order they were named, and one built with a single position returns just that one value from whatever it is given.
questions.hint: Write out the three rows sorted by the number alone before adding the direction.

questions.stem:
Seven readings are summarised by a statistics module, and the mean is also computed by dividing the total by the count and then scaled to whole hundredths. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

import statistics

v = [3, 1, 4, 1, 5, 9, 2]
print(len(v), sum(v))
print(statistics.median(v), statistics.median_low(v), statistics.median_high(v))
print(statistics.mode(v), v.count(statistics.mode(v)))
print(round(statistics.mean(v) * 100))
print(statistics.pstdev(v) < statistics.stdev(v))

options.text: A count of seven with a total of twenty five, a median of three with the low and high forms also reporting three, a mode of one occurring twice, a mean scaled to hundredths of three hundred and fifty seven, and a true comparison of the two spreads

A count of seven with a total of twenty five, a median line reporting three hundred and fifty seven where the median belongs, a mode of one occurring twice, a mean scaled to hundredths of three hundred and fifty seven, and a true comparison of the two spreads
options.misconception: believes a median is the mean of the whole set

options.text: A count of seven with a total of twenty five, a median of three with the low and high forms also three, a mode line reporting one alongside the middle value of three, a mean scaled to hundredths of three hundred and fifty seven, and a true comparison of the spreads
options.misconception: believes the mode is the most frequent rank rather than the value

options.text: A count of seven with a total of twenty five, a median of three with the low and high forms also three, a mode line reporting nine alongside a count of one, a mean scaled to hundredths of three hundred and fifty seven, and a true comparison of the spreads
options.misconception: believes the mode is the largest value in the data

questions.explanation: The mean is the total divided by the count, so the module and the hand-rolled line agree exactly, and scaling it to hundredths turns the repeating value into a whole number that can be checked against the sum. The median of an odd number of readings is the middle reading, so the median and its low and high forms all report the same thing here, which is exactly the case where the distinction between them does not show. The two spreads differ only in the divisor, whole data against one less than the count, so the smaller divisor gives the larger figure and the comparison comes out true. The mode is the most frequent value, which is one and it occurs twice, not the largest value and not the middle one.
questions.hint: Sort the seven values and read the middle one, then divide the total by the count.

questions.topic: Why A Reusable Accessor Beats A Lambda Key
questions.learningObjective: explain what a field accessor gives over a one-line key function
questions.stem:
Three objects with one field are sorted twice, once with a reusable accessor for that field and once with a one-line function. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. Which statement about the two is correct?

import operator

class P:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.n = n

    def __repr__(self):
        return f"P{self.n}"

objs = [P(2), P(1), P(3)]
print([o.n for o in sorted(objs, key=operator.attrgetter("n"))])
print(max(objs, key=operator.attrgetter("n")).n)
print([o.n for o in sorted(objs, key=lambda o: o.n)] == [1, 2, 3])

options.text: Both orderings agree but the largest field is three, and the accessor is chosen because it returns a copy of the field rather than the field itself
options.misconception: believes a field accessor returns a copy of the value

options.text: Both orderings agree and the largest field is three, because a reusable accessor does the same read a one-line function would and costs nothing to keep around
Both orderings agree but the largest field is one, because a reusable accessor sorts by the field and a one-line function sorts by the object
options.misconception: believes a reusable accessor compares objects rather than fields

options.text: The two orderings never both run, because an accessor built for a field the objects do not have stops the program with an AttributeError
options.misconception: believes the two read different fields

questions.explanation: A field accessor is a small object that reads one named field, so handing it to a sort key is the same as handing over a one-line function that reads that field, and the two orderings agree. The reason to prefer the accessor is that it can be built once and reused, and that the field name is written in one place instead of at every call site. It does not copy the value, it does not read a different field from a closure, and it compares exactly what the one-line function would compare. A nested path can be named too, which is the one thing a one-line function needs an extra helper for when the field is several hops away.
questions.hint: Ask what value each key function returns for the same object.

print([m.size for m in sm.get_matching_blocks()])

options.misconception: believes a changed character is reported as a delete with no matching insert

options.text: An equal block, an insert before the third character, then another equal block, matching block sizes of two, one and zero, and a line diff that adds the d without dropping anything
options.misconception: believes a changed character is reported as an insert with no matching delete

options.text: An equal block, a replace of the third character, then another equal block, matching block sizes of two, one and zero, and a line diff that drops the c and adds the d
A single replace covering all four positions, matching block sizes of zero and zero and zero, and a line diff that drops the whole first string and adds the whole second

questions.topic: Where A Search Begins And Where A Match Begins
questions.learningObjective: distinguish a search that scans from a match anchored at the start
questions.stem:
Two letters and then two digits are searched for a run of digits, and a start-at-the-front form is tried on the same text. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

import re

text = "ab12"
print(re.search(r"\d+", text).group())
print(re.match(r"\d+", text))
print(re.search(r"\d+", text).span())
print(re.search(r"\d+", text) is not None, re.match(r"\d+", text) is None)

options.text: The twelve, then the run of letters at the front because a front-anchored form also scans for a pattern that fits later, then the span from two to four, and true for the search and true for the absence of a front match for digits
options.misconception: believes a front-anchored form also scans the whole text

options.text: The twelve, then the absent marker, then the span from zero to two, and true for the search and true for the absence of a front match
options.misconception: believes the reported span is measured from the start of the text

options.text: The twelve, then the absent marker, then the span from two to four, and true for the search and false for the absence of a front match
options.misconception: believes a front form that found nothing still returns a result

options.text: The twelve, then the absent marker because the front of the text is a letter, then the span from two to four, and true for the search and true for the absence of a front match

questions.explanation: A search scans forward through the text and stops at the first place the pattern fits, so it finds the run of digits starting at position two and reports the span from two to four. A front-anchored form only tries position zero, and the character there is a letter, so the pattern does not fit and the result is the absent marker rather than a match. That is why the last line reports true for the search being present and true for the front form being absent. The span is a pair of offsets into the text, not a pair of character values, which is the belief the third answer makes.
questions.hint: Ask where in the text the run of digits actually begins, and what a front-anchored form is allowed to try.

questions.topic: Why A Front Form Cannot Look Further Right
questions.learningObjective: say what a front-anchored pattern form guarantees and does not
questions.stem:
A pattern for two letters and a digit is applied to a four-character text in three ways, and the results are compared. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. Which statement about the front-anchored form is correct?

import re

text = "ab12"
print(re.search(r"[a-z]\d", text).group())
print(re.match(r"a\w", text).group())
print(re.fullmatch(r"[a-z]\d+", text) is None)

options.text: The front-anchored form found ab here, and in general it either matches at the start or reports nothing at all, because it is only ever allowed to try the first position
The front-anchored form found b1 here, and in general it matches the leftmost place the pattern fits, because it scans just as a search does
options.misconception: believes a front-anchored form scans the whole text

options.text: The front-anchored form found ab here, and in general it hands back the boundaries of each part of the pattern so a caller could carry on from there, which is what the middle line shows
options.misconception: believes a front-anchored form hands back a marker for the caller to follow

options.text: The front-anchored form found ab here, and in general it agrees with a search unless the pattern is anchored, in which case the anchoring is silently dropped and the last line reports nothing
options.misconception: believes an anchor is silently ignored

questions.explanation: A front-anchored form is the same machinery as a search with the starting position pinned to the beginning, so it tries exactly one place and either the pattern fits there or nothing is returned. Here the pattern asks for a lower-case letter followed by a digit, the search finds it at positions one and two, and the front-anchored form is given a different pattern that does fit at position zero, which is why it reports something. The third line shows the opposite case, where a form that must cover the whole text finds that the text has four characters and the pattern allows only two, so there is nothing. A full-cover form is a different tool from a front-anchored one, and neither one ever scans.
questions.hint: Ask how many starting positions a front-anchored form is allowed to try.

questions.learningObjective: read the shape a find-all call returns for different group counts
questions.stem:
The same text is searched for digits with no group, then with one letter group and a one-digit group, and the width of a returned pair is measured. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

import re

text = "a1 bb22 ccc333"
print(re.findall(r"\d+", text))
print(re.findall(r"([a-z])(\d)", text))
print(len(re.findall(r"([a-z])(\d)", text)[0]))

options.text: Three whole matches as text, then three pairs of a letter and a digit, and a pair width of two, because naming groups is believed to remove the runs of digits from the first line
options.misconception: believes naming groups changes the results of the ungrouped pattern

options.text: Three whole matches as text, then three pairs of a letter and a single digit, and a pair width of two, because a single group returns text while more than one returns the groups
Whole matches as text, then pairs of a letter with the whole run of digits beside it, and a pair width of two, because the digit group is believed to take the whole run
options.misconception: believes a digit group takes the whole run of digits

options.text: Whole matches as text, then three pairs of a letter and a digit, and a pair width of one, because a find-all call is believed to return only the first named group
options.misconception: believes a find-all call returns only the first named group

questions.explanation: A find-all call returns a list whose shape depends on how many groups the pattern names. With no group each entry is the whole matched text, so the three runs come back whole. With groups the entries become tuples holding one value per named group, and each group is what its own pattern piece matched: the single letter that sits just before the run, and the single digit the digit group is written to take. A run of two or three digits therefore contributes one digit to its group and nothing more, since the group matched once and the scan resumed after it. The width of a pair is the number of named groups, which is two, and that is the same for every entry in the list.
questions.hint: Ask how many characters the digit group is allowed to match inside a run of two digits.

questions.topic: A Greedy Quantifier Takes The Longest Run
questions.learningObjective: read what a greedy quantifier captures in a repeated pattern
questions.stem:
Two angle-bracket pairs are captured by a pattern whose quantifier is greedy, and a quoted phrase is captured by a second greedy pattern. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

import re

print(re.findall(r"<.+>", "<a><b>"))
print(re.findall(r'"[^"]*"', 'say "hi" now'))
print(re.findall(r"a.*b", "axb ayb"))
print(len(re.findall(r"<.*>", "<a><b>")))

options.text: A single greedy capture holding both bracketed pairs together, a list of bare fragments with empty strings between them for the quoted phrase, a single capture spanning from the first a to the last b, and an entry count of one, because a negated class can match an empty run
options.misconception: believes a negated class can match an empty run of text

options.text: A greedy capture holding both bracketed pairs together, a capture holding the quoted phrase, a capture spanning from the first a to the last b, and an entry count of two, because the two patterns are believed to be counted together rather than separately
options.misconception: believes the two patterns are counted together

options.text: A single greedy capture holding both bracketed pairs together, a single capture holding the quoted phrase, a single capture spanning from the first a to the last b, and an entry count of one, because a greedy quantifier takes as much as it can
Captures holding a bracketed pair each, a capture holding the quoted phrase, and an entry count of two, because a lazy quantifier is believed to stop as soon as the rest of the pattern can match
options.misconception: believes a greedy quantifier stops as early as the rest of the pattern allows

questions.explanation: A greedy quantifier is written to take as much as it can and then hand control to the rest of the pattern, so a run of any characters between two angle brackets swallows the first closing bracket as well and the capture ends at the last one. That is why the two pairs come back as a single entry rather than two. The quoted phrase behaves the same way but stops earlier because the closing quote character is excluded by the class, so the run cannot cross it. The third pattern has no excluded character at all, so it runs from the first a all the way to the last b, and the whole run matches only once, which the final count confirms.
questions.hint: Ask which characters the run between the brackets is allowed to include.

The third line counts the same way for the same reason: the run from a to b stops at the first b, so the two candidates produce two matches. questions.stem:
A three-letter word is searched for with boundary assertions on both sides, first inside a phrase and then inside a longer word, and it is then substituted for before a whole-word length pattern is run on the same text. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

import re

text = "a cat category concat"
print(re.findall(r"\bcat\b", text))
print(re.search(r"\bcat\b", "concat") is None)
print(re.sub(r"\bcat\b", "dog", text))
print(re.findall(r"\b\w{3}\b", text))

options.misconception: believes a trailing boundary still matches inside a longer word

options.text: A single match for the standalone word, an absent result inside the longer word, a substitution that changes only the standalone word, and a longer list of bare character runs, because the length pattern is believed to ignore the boundaries
options.misconception: believes the length pattern ignores the boundaries

options.text: A single match for the standalone word, an absent result inside the longer word, a substitution that changes only the standalone word, and a last line of whole words that are not changed by the substitution, because a trailing boundary is believed to survive it
options.misconception: believes a length pattern cannot be combined with boundaries

questions.explanation: A boundary assertion says that the position next to it is the edge between a word character and something else, so the leading one fails inside a longer word where the letters continue, and the trailing one fails where a letter follows. That is why the standalone occurrence is found and the one inside the longer word is not, and why the substitution leaves the longer word untouched. The last line then runs on the text as it now stands, and the word has already become a different one, so the count of whole three-letter words drops to a single entry. That ordering is the trap: the same program would report a different last line if the two steps were swapped.

questions.learningObjective: read a substitution whose replacement is computed by a function
questions.stem:
Three substitutions are run, one that upper-cases each word, one that puts each captured digit in front of its letter, and one that squeezes runs of spaces. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

import re

def shout(m):
    return m.group(0).upper()

print(re.sub(r"\w+", shout, "ab cd"))
print(re.sub(r"(\w)(\d)", lambda m: m.group(2) + m.group(1), "a1 b2"))
print(re.sub(r"\s+", " ", "a  b   c"))

options.text: AB CD, then 1a 2b, then a  b  c, because the squeezing pattern is believed to leave more than one space behind
options.misconception: believes a squeeze pattern leaves a run of spaces rather than a single space

options.text: AB CD, then 1a 2b, then a b c, because the replacement is computed for each match from the groups the pattern captured
ab cd ab cd on the first line, then 1a 2b, then a b c, because the function is believed to be handed the whole text once and its return value replaces every match
options.misconception: believes the function receives the whole text rather than one match

options.text: AB CD, then a1 b2, then a b c, because the group references are believed to be emitted in the order the pattern matched rather than the order it names
options.misconception: believes the group references come back in match order rather than name order

questions.explanation: When the replacement is a function it is called once per match and what it returns becomes the replacement for that match, and it is handed the match object so it can read whichever groups the pattern named. That is why the letters and digits swap places in the second line, and why the third line collapses each run of whitespace down to a single space rather than removing the spaces entirely. The first line is the simplest case: the function ignores the groups and upper-cases whatever it was given, so the result differs from the input only in case. A function replacement is the tool to reach for when the new text cannot be written as a fixed template.
questions.hint: Ask how many times the function is called, and what it is handed each time.

questions.topic: The Order A Format Specification Is Read In
questions.learningObjective: state the order the parts of a format specification are read in
questions.stem:
Four specifications are written and compared, and the first one is inspected character by character. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does that tell you about the order the parts are read in?

print(format(7, "08.3f") + "|", format(7.5, "+07.2f") + "|")

answer.exemplar: The parts are read in a fixed order and a specification is a sequence rather than a set of switches that can be given in any order. The order is the fill character, then the alignment, then the sign, then the zero pad, then the width, then the grouping, then the precision, and finally the type. A specification is therefore easy to misread by eye because a fill character and an alignment character look like an ordinary number: a leading digit is a fill only when another digit follows it, so four followed by a type is a width while zero followed by a digit is a zero pad with the digit as the width. That is also why a sign can only appear once the alignment has been settled, and why a precision has to come before the type it belongs to. The practical habit is to read a specification from the right to left when checking it: the type first, then the precision, then the width, then everything else, because that is the order in which the pieces are consumed.

A leading digit is only a fill character when it is followed by an alignment character, so a specification that begins with a digit and a second digit is a width while a specification that begins with a zero and a digit is a zero pad. Reading from the right is the reliable check: the type, then the precision, then the width, then the sign, then the alignment and the fill. A specification that is out of order is not silently rearranged, it is rejected.
questions.hint: Read a specification from the right, taking the type first and the fill last.

questions.stem:
An integer square root is taken for three nearby values and for a large one, and it is compared with a float root converted to an integer. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

import math

print(math.isqrt(50), math.isqrt(49), math.isqrt(51))
print(int(50 ** 0.5), math.isqrt(50) == int(50 ** 0.5))
print(math.isqrt(10 ** 12))
print(math.isqrt(50) ** 2 <= 50, (math.isqrt(50) + 1) ** 2 > 50)

options.text: The same whole root for the nearby values, a float root that agrees with it here, a root of a million for a large value, and only the second bracketing test true, because the root is allowed to overshoot the input
options.misconception: believes the root may overshoot the input

options.text: The same whole root for the nearby values, a float root that agrees with it here, a root of a million for a large value, and both bracketing tests true, because the nearby values are each believed to be rounded to a root of their own
options.misconception: believes each input is rounded to its own root

options.text: The same whole root for the nearby values, a float root that agrees with it here, a root of a million for a large value, and both bracketing tests true, because the root is the largest whole value whose square does not exceed the input

The same whole root for the nearby values, a float root that agrees with it here, a root of a million for a large value, and both bracketing tests true, because the root is taken to be the smallest whole value whose square is at least the input
options.misconception: believes the root is the smallest value whose square is large enough

questions.explanation: The integer square root is the largest whole value whose square does not exceed the input, so every value between one square and the next below it gives the same answer, which is why three nearby values all come out the same. The two bracketing tests are the definition written out: squaring the root does not exceed the input, and squaring the next whole value up does. A float root converted to an integer happens to agree here, but it is not the same operation, because a float root of a large enough value is not exactly representable and can land on the wrong side of the boundary. That is why a program dealing with sizes should ask for the integer root directly.
questions.hint: Ask whether the root is the largest or the smallest whole value that fits, and write both bracketing tests.

questions.topic: One Division Returning Both Parts
questions.learningObjective: read a quotient and remainder for negative operands
questions.stem:
One division is asked for both its parts with three different signs, and the parts are also computed separately for comparison. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

print(divmod(17, 5), divmod(-17, 5), divmod(17, -5))
print(17 // 5, 17 % 5, -17 // 5, -17 % 5)
print(divmod(100, 10))
print(divmod(-17, 5)[1] > 0)

options.text: A quotient of 3 with a remainder of 2, a quotient of -3 with a remainder of -2, a quotient of -3 with a remainder of -2, the same figures computed separately, an exact division whose remainder is 0, and a true test that the remainder follows the sign of the dividend
options.misconception: believes the remainder takes the sign of the dividend

options.text: A quotient of 3 with a remainder of 2, a quotient of -4 with a remainder of 3, a quotient of -3 with a remainder of 2, the same figures computed separately, an exact division whose remainder is 0, and a true test that the remainder follows the sign of the divisor
options.misconception: believes the quotient always rounds towards zero

options.text: A quotient of 3 with a remainder of 2, a quotient of -4 with a remainder of 3, a quotient of -4 with a remainder of -3, the same figures computed separately, an exact division whose remainder is the divisor itself, and a true test that the remainder follows the sign of the divisor
options.misconception: believes an exact division still reports the divisor as the remainder

options.text: A quotient of 3 with a remainder of 2, a quotient of -4 with a remainder of 3, a quotient of -4 with a remainder of -3, the same figures computed separately, an exact division whose remainder is 0, and a true test that the remainder follows the sign of the divisor

questions.explanation: The division here is a floor division, which means the quotient is rounded down rather than towards zero, and the remainder is whatever is left over with the sign of the divisor. So seventeen over five is a quotient of three and a remainder of two, and negative seventeen over five is a quotient of negative four and a remainder of positive three, because subtracting negative four fives from negative seventeen leaves positive three. The sign rule is worth stating because it surprises people: the remainder is never negative when the divisor is positive, which is exactly what makes the floor division total back to the original. A division with no remainder gives a remainder of zero, not the divisor.
questions.hint: Write the division as the quotient times the divisor plus the remainder, and check the signs.

questions.topic: Which Way A Tie Rounds
questions.learningObjective: say which way a rounding tie is resolved and why
questions.stem:
Six values are rounded to a whole number and two are rounded to two places, and the values written in the source are printed beside them. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. Which statement about the rounding is correct?

print(round(2.5), round(3.5), round(0.5), round(1.5), round(-2.5), round(-1.5))
print(round(2.675, 2), 2.675)
print(round(1.005, 2), 1.005)
print(2.5 == round(2.5), 3.5 == round(3.5))

options.text: A tie lands on whichever neighbouring value has an even last digit, and the two-place figures come from the stored value rather than from the written one
A tie is always rounded upwards, and the two-place figures come from the stored value rather than from the written one
options.misconception: believes a tie is always rounded up

options.text: A tie lands on whichever neighbouring value has an even last digit, and the two-place figures come from the written decimal rather than from the stored value
options.misconception: believes the two-place figures come from the written decimal

options.text: A tie is rounded away from zero, and the two-place figures come from the stored value rather than from the written one
options.misconception: believes a tie is rounded away from zero

questions.explanation: A rounding tie has no preferred direction here, so the rule is to keep the value whose final digit is even, which is why the value between 2 and 3 lands on 2 and the value between 3 and 4 lands on 4, and why the value between -2 and -1 lands on -2. The choice is arbitrary in the sense that any consistent rule would do, but a consistent rule is the point: the same input always gives the same output, and a long run of additions does not drift upwards the way rounding each step up would. The two-place figures are a separate matter, because the value being rounded is the one that is stored, and the stored form of the written 2.675 is slightly below it, which is why rounding it to two places gives 2.67 rather than 2.68.
questions.hint: Ask which of the two neighbouring values has an even last digit, and whether the value being rounded is the written one.

questions.topic: Bits Cut Out Of One Integer
questions.learningObjective: apply bit operations to a small integer and read the result
questions.stem:
One small binary value is combined with another in four ways, then shifted and measured. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. What does it print?

print(0b1010 | 0b0101, 0b1010 & 0b0101, 0b1010 ^ 0b0101, ~0b1010)
print(1 << 10, 1024 >> 3, (0b1010).bit_length(), (0b1010).bit_count())
print(0b1010 & 0x0F, 0b1010 | 0x0F, 0b1010 ^ 0xFF)

options.text: 15 where either bit is set, 0 where both must be set, 15 where they differ, and -11 for the complement, then a left shift to 1024, a right shift to 128, a bit length of 4 with 3 set bits, and the masked results 10, 15 and 245
options.misconception: believes the set-bit count includes a bit that is not set

options.text: 15 where either bit is set, 0 where both must be set, 15 where they differ, and -11 for the complement, then a left shift to 1024, a right shift to 128, a bit length of 4 with 2 set bits, and the masked results 10, 15 and 245

15 where either bit is set, 10 where both must be set, 5 where they differ, and 5 for the complement, then a left shift to 1024, a right shift to 128, a bit length of 4 with 2 set bits, and the masked results 10, 15 and 245
options.misconception: believes the complement of a small value is its reverse

options.text: 15 where either bit is set, 0 where both must be set, 15 where they differ, and -11 for the complement, then a left shift to a value with far more digits, a right shift to 128, a bit length of 5 with 2 set bits, and the masked results 10, 15 and 245
options.misconception: believes a left shift moves two decimal places

questions.explanation: A bit operation treats the number as a row of switches rather than as a quantity, so the inclusive or keeps a bit set when either side has it, the conjunction keeps one only when both do, and the exclusive or keeps one when they differ. The complement has no upper limit, so it flips every bit including the sign bit and comes out negative, which is why negating a small number gives a large negative one rather than a small positive one. A left shift multiplies by two for each place and a right shift divides, the bit length counts the places from the top bit down to one, and the set-bit count counts the bits that are on. Masking with a low mask keeps the low four bits, which is how a small field is carved out of a larger value.
questions.hint: Write both values out as rows of bits and read each operation off the rows.

questions.subject: PYTHON
questions.topic: How Many Groups A Combination Forms
questions.learningObjective: count unordered groups of a fixed size and cross-check with a closed form
questions.stem:
A program forms every unordered group of three from six distinct values, counts them by building the whole list, and checks the count against a closed form. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. Both figures it prints agree. What number is that count?

import itertools
import math

vals = ["a", "b", "c", "d", "e", "f"]
groups = list(itertools.combinations(vals, 3))
print(len(groups))
print(math.comb(6, 3))
print(len(groups) == math.comb(6, 3))
questions.explanation: Every unordered group of three out of six values is produced once, because the order of the three values inside a group does not matter and the generator emits each choice in a fixed order, so no group is repeated. The count is the number of ways to choose three positions out of six, which is six times five times four divided by three times two times one, because each group would be counted once for each of the six orders its three values can appear in. That division is what turns an ordered count into an unordered one, and it is why the closed form carries a factorial in the denominator. Building the whole list and asking the closed form give the same figure, which is the check worth writing whenever a counting routine and a formula are both available.
questions.hint: Choose three of the six positions, then divide by the number of orders each group can appear in.

questions.topic: A Paragraph Cut To A Column Width
questions.learningObjective: pair the lines a wrapping helper produces with the reason the tail came out as it did
questions.stem:
A paragraph of nine words is cut to lines of at most twelve characters, and the last line and the line count are reported. The program below is run under CPython 3.14.3. Which pair names what this program prints and why?

import textwrap

para = "the quick brown fox jumps over the lazy dog"
print(textwrap.wrap(para, width=12))
print(textwrap.wrap(para, width=12)[-1])
print(len(textwrap.wrap(para, width=12)))

options.text: Nine lines ending in the dog, because the helper is believed to fill each line to exactly the width rather than to at most the width
options.misconception: believes each line is filled to exactly the width

options.text: Four lines whose first entry carries a prefix and whose third line is shorter, because the helper is believed to add a prefix of its own to the first line
options.misconception: believes the helper adds a prefix of its own to the first line

options.text: Four lines ending in the lazy dog, because words are kept whole and the last line is allowed to be shorter than the width
Three lines whose last entry ends in an ellipsis marker, because the helper is believed to stop after a fixed number of lines
options.misconception: believes the helper stops after a fixed number of lines

questions.explanation: The wrapping helper takes a width as a limit rather than a target, so it packs whole words until the next one would not fit and then starts a new line. The last line is therefore allowed to be shorter, and here it is the shortest of the four, which is what tells you the words were kept whole. The line count follows from the widths rather than from the number of words, because each line holds as many words as fit, which is why halving the width roughly doubles the count. A trailing line break in the value is the thing to watch for in other programs, since it can add an empty line.
questions.hint: Decide whether the width is a limit or a target, and whether a word may be split.
